newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala invites bids for telecom sale by Aug.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala invites bids for telecom sale by Aug.

text.p: Guatemala has invited international companies to take part in the sale of its state-owned telephone company and to place their bids by early August.
"It is an invitation to international operators to prequalify," Alfredo Guzman, manager of the Guatemalan Telecommunications Company (Guatel), told a news conference late on Friday.
The invitation, published in major foreign newspapers, calls for qualified bidders -- operators or operating consortiums with experience in telecommunications services -- to apply.
"This guarantees us that they will be world class businesses, experts in the area and successsful," Guzman said.
The government aims to raise hundreds of millions of dollars, improve service and build up the country's telephone network with the Guatel sale.
Guatel operates only 350,000 phone lines in the small Central American country of 10 million people.
Interested companies have three weeks to submit prequalifying material to J.P. Morgan Securities, which is advising the Guatemalan government on the Guatel sale.
In a late May road show, representatives of Guatel and J.P. Morgan visited Spain's Telefonica de Espana, Italy's Stet, France Telecom, and U.S. firms GTE Corp and MCI Communications Corp.
"At the time they all showed interest, but in the next two weeks we will see who has real interest and submits the paperwork," Guzman said.
The buyer will have the option of a 51 to 95 percent stake in the company. The shares are currently held in a trust, and will be handed over to the buyer after the sale.
The remaining five percent of the shares will be offered to Guatel employees, Guzman said.
Guzman said he hopes to receive bids and close the transaction by the third quarter of this year.

The value of Guatel has been the source of widely varying rumors in the Guatemalan press. A source close to the sale told Reuters that published numbers of $200 million and $1 billion were both unrealistic.
The same source said that a benchmark figure of $2,000 a line yields a value of $700 million, but added that the value would be determined by the market.
Telephone systems in Brazil and Panama have sold for a greater price per line, while other phone systems have gone for much less.
